edges.effect_quant: Randomized ACT-based lifestyle programs improved diabetes self-care over 3 months and more than doubled the observed 30-day quit rate in a web smoking-cessation trial (23% vs 10%; OR 3.05, 95% CI 1.01-9.32), but a large head-to-head smoking trial found ACT and CBT had similar 12-month abstinence rates (13.8% vs 18.1%; adjusted OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.35-1.27).
edges.population: adults receiving acceptance and commitment therapy applied to smoking, diabetes self-management, or other lifestyle behaviors
edges.mechanism: Acceptance and commitment therapy tries to improve behavior by reducing experiential avoidance and helping people act in line with chosen values even when cravings, stress, or self-criticism are still present. That can support self-management and quitting efforts, but the behavioral advantage is often modest and sometimes comparable to other structured counseling models.
edges.summary: The overall picture is directionally positive: ACT-based lifestyle interventions can improve targeted health behaviors, especially self-management and smoking-related outcomes. The strongest caveat is that ACT does not consistently outperform other credible behavioral therapies, so the edge is better read as helpful than uniquely powerful.
edges.caveats: This category bundles different delivery formats and goals, from diabetes groups to web smoking programs to group counseling against CBT. Positive results in one context do not mean ACT will dominate every behavior-change comparison, especially when the alternative arm is an active evidence-based treatment rather than minimal support.

evidence.notes: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for Type 2 Diabetes Management: The Moderating Role of Coping Styles.
